screens.title: Making HTTP Requests with Fetch API
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn to use the Fetch A P I, the native JavaScript interface for making HTTP requests inside React Native. We'll explain how to perform common operations: retrieve data with GET, send data with POST and PUT, and remove data with DELETE. You'll learn why awaiting both the fetch call and the response. json call matters, how to inspect response. ok and response. status to detect HTTP errors, and how to set headers and stringify JSON for request bodies. The practical examples use a mock A P I so you can see responses and update local state even when the remote service does not persist changes. We'll also cover basic error handling patterns and a simple timeout strategy using Promise. race so your app can fail fast when a server is slow. By the end you will be able to wire a component to fetch data on mount, show loading and error states, and perform safe updates using the Fetch A P I. Think about one component you will add fetch to — what data will it request and how will you handle a 500 response? That question will guide your hands-on work.

Making HTTP Requests with Fetch API

A compact, practical guide to fetching JSON, sending payloads, and handling errors in React Native using the native Fetch API.

16:9 HD Classroom
In this lesson
GET data from APIs and display it with state and useEffect.
Coming up
Send JSON payloads using POST/PUT and set Content-Type headers.
Practice
A hands-on To-Do example shows updates via PUT and deletions via DELETE.
Concept Cards
Request & Response
Request options shape what you send; inspect response.ok to detect HTTP errors.
JSON Handling
Await both fetch and response.json to get parsed objects.
Why it matters
Reliable networking code prevents subtle bugs where a Promise is left unresolved or an HTTP error is treated as success.
Quick Topics
GET requests
Retrieve lists and objects; used with useEffect to fetch on mount.
POST / PUT / DELETE
Send JSON payloads, update resources, and remove items using options.method.
Error handling
Check response.ok and handle network errors separately; consider timeouts.
Explore these topics in the next slides as live-coding examples and hands-on practice.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives describe the practical skills you will acquire using the Fetch A P I in React Native. First, you will be able to perform basic GET requests and display the returned JSON data using state and lifecycle hooks, which matters because most apps need remote data. Second, you will construct POST, PUT, and DELETE requests with a proper options object including method, headers, and body; this lets you create and update resources on an A P I and practice safe payload formatting. Third, you will parse responses correctly by awaiting response. json and using response. ok and response. status to detect HTTP errors — a common source of bugs if left unchecked. Fourth, you will implement basic error handling patterns and a simple timeout approach so your UI responds when networks fail or servers are slow. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic to help you remember the workflow and a milestone indicator showing when competency is verified. Together these skills let you build components that fetch, display, and update remote data reliably.

screens.title: What is the Fetch API?
screens.narratorSegment: The Fetch A P I is a native JavaScript interface that defines how to perform HTTP network requests and work with the returned responses. In React Native it is available without additional libraries, and it gives you Request and Response objects that are more flexible than older techniques. A Request describes what you want to send — the URL, method, headers, and optional body — and the Response encapsulates status, headers, and body text. Practically, you call fetch with a URL and an optional options object. The fetch call returns a Promise that resolves to a Response. That Response is not yet the parsed JSON; you must call response. json and await it to obtain the object. A common misconception is to assume that fetch rejects on any HTTP error; in reality fetch rejects only on network failures, so you need to check response. ok to treat non-2xx responses as errors. For example, if you request a user list and the server responds 404, fetch resolves, and you must inspect response. status or response. ok and handle it. The takeaway is: fetch gives you control, but you must explicitly parse and verify responses before using the data. How will you check response. ok in your next component?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What is the Fetch API?
Core Concept

Fetch API: Request & Response

Fetch is a native modern alternative to older HTTP techniques. It returns a Response which you must inspect and parse.

Request object
Describes the operation: url, method, headers, and body. Use it to configure POST and PUT payloads.
Response object
Contains status, statusText, headers, and functions like response.json() to parse the body.
Common mistake
Assuming fetch rejects on HTTP errors. Always check response.ok and response.status.
Concept Visual
Short annotated example of the Request → Response flow.
<!-- Example: simple GET flow -->
const response = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users');
// Check HTTP status
if (!response.ok) {
  throw new Error(`HTTP error! status: ${response.status}`);
}
const data = await response.json();
// data is now a parsed JavaScript array or object
Key Takeaway

Always await both fetch and response.json, and treat non-2xx responses as errors.

Check your understanding
What happens if you forget to await response.json? How will you detect a 404 from the server?

screens.title: GET requests and useEffect
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical GET example you can copy into a React Native component. The pattern uses useEffect to trigger the fetch once when the component mounts and useState to hold data, loading, and error states. Start by calling fetch with the endpoint URL. After awaiting the fetch, immediately check response. ok. If it's false, throw an error that your catch block can handle. Then await response. json to parse the body. Use the parsed array to set state and flip loading to false in finally. This approach keeps the UI responsive: you show an activity indicator while loading, display a readable error message if something goes wrong, and render the FlatList when data is present. A common pitfall is forgetting to await response. json, which leaves json as a Promise. Another subtle issue is not guarding the component for unmounted state in longer-lived requests, but for short example fetches this pattern is solid. Practice by fetching the sample users endpoint and rendering names and emails. After that, ask yourself: how do you surface a 500 error versus a network failure in your UI?

keyIdea.title: GET pattern
keyIdea.text: Use useEffect + fetch + response.ok check + await response.json + state updates to render remote data safely.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › GET requests and useEffect
Process

Fetch on mount and render list

Follow this exact pattern to avoid common mistakes and show good UI states.

// UsersScreen.js (excerpt)
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

useEffect(() => {
  const fetchUsers = async () => {
    try {
      const response = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users');
      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`HTTP error! status: ${response.status}`);
      }
      const json = await response.json();
      setUsers(json);
    } catch (e) {
      setError(e.message);
    } finally {
      setLoading(false);
    }
  };
  fetchUsers();
}, []);
Key Takeaway

Await fetch and response.json, check response.ok, and update loading and error state in finally.

Example UI behavior
While loading show an ActivityIndicator. On error show a friendly message. On success render a FlatList of items.
Simulated Output
This panel shows what your FlatList would render after fetching users: each item includes name and email.

Fetch will reject on HTTP 404 or 500. Actually, fetch resolves; you must check response.ok and handle non-2xx statuses yourself.

screens.title: Parsing JSON: await response.json()
screens.narratorSegment: Parsing JSON from a Response is a two-step asynchronous process: first you await fetch which yields a Response object, then you call response. json which itself returns a Promise that resolves to the parsed JavaScript value. If you forget the second await, your variable will hold a Promise instead of the expected array or object; using that Promise like data will lead to runtime errors or empty renderings. In practice always write const json = await response. json(); and consider wrapping that in a try/catch if the server returns malformed JSON. Another detail: when an HTTP error occurs, the response body might contain an error payload; you can attempt to parse it with response. json but guard with try/catch because error bodies are not guaranteed to be JSON. A concrete strategy: after fetch resolves check response. ok, and if false attempt to parse errorBody = await response. json(). Use that information to build a user-facing message. The takeaway: treat parsing as part of the network flow and always await the parse step to avoid unresolved Promises in your state. Parsing JSON: await response.json() means response.json() returns a promise. always await it and guard against malformed or non-json error bodies.. In practical terms, why awaiting response.json matters and how to avoid the promise pitfall. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Parsing JSON: await response.json()
Definition

Await the parser

response.json returns a Promise that resolves to the parsed object; forgetting to await it yields bugs.

const response = await fetch(url);
if (!response.ok) {
  // Optionally parse an error body
  let errMsg = `Status ${response.status}`;
  try {
    const errorBody = await response.json();
    errMsg = errorBody.message || errMsg;
  } catch (parseErr) {
    // body not JSON
  }
  throw new Error(errMsg);
}
const data = await response.json();
Analogy
Think of fetch as the delivery van and response.json as unpacking and assembling the boxes into usable parts.
Common Pitfall
If you set state to the result of response.json without awaiting, your UI may render a Promise object or crash. Always await the parse step before setState.
Concrete example
Bad: setData(response.json()); Good: const data = await response.json(); setData(data);
Key Takeaway

Await response.json() and guard parsing for error bodies that might not be valid JSON.

Check your understanding
If a server returns a 500 with an HTML error page, what happens when you call response.json()?

screens.title: POST, PUT, DELETE: using the options object
screens.narratorSegment: To send or modify data you supply a second argument to fetch: the options object. This object commonly includes method, headers, and body. For JSON payloads set headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'} and use JSON. stringify to convert your JavaScript object into a string. For a POST you typically include the object you want to create, for PUT you send the updated resource, and for DELETE you can omit the body or include minimal identifying data. After calling fetch with these options, remember the same response checks and parsing patterns: if (! response. ok) handle the server-side error, otherwise await response. json for the response body. A frequent beginner mistake is to pass a plain object as body without stringifying, which leads to incorrect request payloads. Another gotcha is forgetting to include Authorization headers when endpoints require authentication. Practice by writing a createPost function that returns the created resource from the server and re-throws errors so the calling component can show a message or update local state. Which mutation will you implement first in your app and how will you verify it updated the UI?

keyIdea.title: Mutation pattern
keyIdea.text: Use fetch(url, { method, headers, body: JSON.stringify(obj) }), check response.ok, await response.json, and update local state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › POST, PUT, DELETE: using the options object
Process Flow

Build the options object for mutations

Step-by-step
  1. Decide method: 'POST' to create, 'PUT' to replace/update, 'DELETE' to remove.
  2. Set headers. For JSON include 'Content-Type': 'application/json'. Add Authorization when required.
  3. Stringify the payload: body: JSON.stringify(payload).
  4. Call fetch(url, options) and await the response, then check response.ok and parse as needed.
  5. Update local state to reflect the mutation and handle errors in catch.
// POST example
const createPost = async (title, body) => {
  const response = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ title, body, userId: 1 }),
  });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP error! status: ${response.status}`);
  return await response.json();
};
Analogy
Think of headers as labels on a package and JSON.stringify as packing the contents into the required format.
Common Mistake

Passing a plain object as body without JSON.stringify will send [object Object] or cause unexpected payloads.

Key Takeaway

Always stringify JSON bodies and set Content-Type so servers parse your payload correctly.

screens.title: Handling HTTP errors vs Network errors
screens.narratorSegment: A crucial part of robust networking is distinguishing between HTTP errors and network errors. Fetch only rejects the returned Promise on network-level failures, such as loss of connectivity or DNS issues. It resolves the Promise when a response is received from the server, even if that response is 404 or 500. That means you cannot rely on the catch block alone to detect bad status codes. Instead, after awaiting fetch, inspect response. ok, which is true for 2xx statuses and false otherwise. For HTTP errors you should parse the response body when helpful and throw a new Error to funnel handling through your catch block. For network errors fetch rejects, so the catch will run directly. A common beginner misconception is to expect fetch to throw on a 404; treating all non-ok responses the same way — by throwing after parsing any error body — yields consistent behavior. A practical pattern is to centralize this check in a small helper that throws when needed so your components only handle errors, not status logic. Handling HTTP errors vs Network errors means check response.ok and response.status after fetch; use try/catch to handle both parsed http errors and network failures consistently.. In practical terms, why fetch resolves for 4xx/5xx and how to treat each case. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Handling HTTP errors vs Network errors
Comparison

HTTP error vs Network error

HTTP error (4xx / 5xx)
fetch resolves; response.ok is false. Parse response body for error details and throw to unify handling.
Network error
fetch rejects immediately. Handle these with catch to show offline or retry UI.
// Unified checker
const checkedFetch = async (url, options) => {
  const response = await fetch(url, options);
  if (!response.ok) {
    let errText = `Status ${response.status}`;
    try { const errBody = await response.json(); errText = errBody.message || errText; } catch(e){}
    throw new Error(errText);
  }
  return await response.json();
};
Practical UX
Show a retry button or a clear error message for HTTP errors, and a distinct offline message when network failure occurs. This helps users understand whether the problem is the server or their connection.
Common Mistake

Relying on catch to detect 404s. Use response.ok to detect server-returned error statuses.

Key Takeaway

Differentiate server errors from network failures and present distinct UI recovery options.

screens.title: Request timeouts and Promise.race
screens.narratorSegment: Fetch does not include a built-in timeout. If a server is slow or unresponsive, a fetch call can hang indefinitely. A simple and practical pattern to avoid this is to race the fetch call against a timeout Promise using Promise. race(). Create a Promise that rejects after a chosen duration and race it with the fetch Promise; when the timeout wins, you handle rejection and update UI accordingly. This approach gives you a fail-fast behavior and a place to show a retry UI. Be mindful that Promise. race does not cancel the original fetch; it only ignores the slower result. For real cancellation you may need AbortController in environments that support it, or a library that exposes cancellation. For basic apps, using Promise. race with a short timeout is usually sufficient to prevent hung network calls and create a predictable UX. Practice implementing a 10-second timeout and decide what fallback message to present to users when the request times out. Request timeouts and Promise.race means use promise.race with a rejecting timeout promise to fail fast when a server is too slow; consider abortcontroller for cancellation when available.. In practical terms, implement a simple timeout for fetch using promise.race. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Request timeouts and Promise.race
Definition

Fail-fast with Promise.race

Race fetch against a timeout Promise that rejects after N milliseconds to avoid indefinite waits.

// Timeout helper
const fetchWithTimeout = (url, options = {}, timeout = 10000) => {
  const timeoutPromise = new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('Request timed out')), timeout)
  );
  return Promise.race([fetch(url, options), timeoutPromise]);
};

// Usage
try {
  const response = await fetchWithTimeout('/slow-endpoint');
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Bad status');
  const data = await response.json();
} catch (e) {
  // handle timeout or network/server errors
}
Note
Promise.race does not cancel the underlying fetch; it simply gives control back to your code sooner.
UX decision
Choose a sensible timeout for your app context. For critical fast interactions shorter timeouts improve perceived performance; for large downloads prefer longer timeouts.
Common Mistake

Assuming Promise.race cancels the fetch. It doesn't; it only resolves/rejects the first Promise.

Key Takeaway

Use Promise.race for simple timeouts; use AbortController or a library when real cancellation is required.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › To-Do example: fetch, mark complete with PUT
Live Coding

Marking a To-Do completed

Send a PUT request and update the local list so users see immediate results even if the server is mock.

const markTodoCompleted = async (id) => {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/${id}`, {
      method: 'PUT',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ completed: true }),
    });

    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP error! status: ${response.status}`);
    const updatedTodo = await response.json();
    setTodos(prev => prev.map(todo => todo.id === id ? { ...todo, completed: updatedTodo.completed } : todo));
    Alert.alert('Success', `Todo ${id} marked as completed (simulated).`);
  } catch (e) {
    Alert.alert('Error', `Failed to update todo: ${e.message}`);
  }
};
Practice prompt
Implement optimistic UI: mark the item completed locally before the server confirms, and rollback on error.
Scenario card
You click 'Mark Completed' and the app immediately marks the item. The PUT request simulates persistence and the UI confirms success via an alert.
Key Takeaway

Update local state after server response or optimistically and rollback on failure to keep the app responsive.

Common Mistake
Not updating local state after a simulated server update, leaving the UI stale even though an operation succeeded.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Delete pattern and updating local state
Process

DELETE and optimistic UI

Implement optimistic removal with rollback to make deletions feel instant while remaining safe on failure.

const deleteTodo = async (id) => {
  const previous = todos;
  setTodos(prev => prev.filter(t => t.id !== id)); // optimistic
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/${id}`, { method: 'DELETE' });
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    // success: keep state updated
  } catch (e) {
    // rollback on failure
    setTodos(previous);
    Alert.alert('Delete failed', e.message);
  }
};
Scenario
User taps Delete; the app removes the item and attempts the network call. If the call fails, the item is restored and the user is informed.
UX trade-offs
Optimistic updates give immediate feedback but require rollback logic. Pessimistic updates wait for server confirmation but feel slower.
Pro Tip

Show a small spinner or disable the delete control while the request is in progress to avoid duplicate requests.

Key Takeaway

Use optimistic removal with clear rollback rules or wait for server confirmation if rollback complexity is high.

screens.title: Limitations of Fetch and when to use a library
screens.narratorSegment: Fetch is intentionally lightweight and built into JavaScript, making it perfect for simple GET and POST operations in many apps. However, it has limitations: no built-in timeout, no request cancellation in some environments without AbortController support, and no built-in retry or interceptor mechanisms for global behavior like attaching tokens or logging. Libraries such as Axios provide convenience features like automatic JSON transformation, request cancellation, timeout defaults, interceptors for authentication headers, and a consistent error shape. That said, adding a library increases bundle size and complexity. The rule of thumb is to start with Fetch for straightforward operations and add a library when you need advanced features such as global request/response interception, retries with backoff, or easier cancellation semantics. In many classroom projects Fetch is sufficient. Before adopting a library, list the problems you need solved — timeouts, retries, cancellation — and prefer the minimal tool that covers them. Which advanced feature would justify adding a library in your project? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison

Fetch vs. Higher-level libraries

Fetch
Built-in, lightweight, suitable for basic GET/POST flows. You manage parsing and checks manually.
Libraries (e.g., Axios)
Provide features like timeouts, interceptors, automatic transforms, and consistent error shapes at the cost of added dependency surface.
Decision checklist
  • Do you need global interceptors for auth tokens?
  • Do you require cancellation and retries out of the box?
  • Is bundle size a concern in your project?
Practical guidance
Start with Fetch. If you find yourself copying the same timeout, retry, or header logic across many files, centralize that into a helper or consider a library that gives you these features cleanly.

Wrap repeated fetch patterns into small helper functions before adding external dependencies.

Choose the simplest tool that solves your real problems; prefer helpers or libraries when you need advanced global features.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Putting it all together: recommended patterns
Architecture

Encapsulate and standardize

Suggested api helper design
// api.js (concept)
export const checkedFetch = async (url, options = {}) => {
  const response = await fetch(url, options);
  if (!response.ok) {
    try { const err = await response.json(); throw new Error(err.message || `Status ${response.status}`); } catch(e) { throw new Error(`Status ${response.status}`); }
  }
  return response.json();
};
This helper centralizes checks and parsing so components only call get/post/put/delete helpers and handle results and errors.
UI patterns
  • Show clear loading indicators and item-level spinners for actions.
  • Display friendly error messages derived from parsed error bodies.
  • Use optimistic updates with rollback where the UX benefits outweigh complexity.
Key Takeaway

Centralize network logic into small helpers to make your components simpler and easier to test or update later.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn to use the Fetch A P I, the native JavaScript interface for making HTTP requests inside React Native. We'll explain how to perform common operations: retrieve data with GET, send data with POST and PUT, and remove data with DELETE. You'll learn why awaiting both the fetch call and the response. json call matters, how to inspect response. ok and response. status to detect HTTP errors, and how to set headers and stringify JSON for request bodies. The practical examples use a mock A P I so you can see responses and update local state even when the remote service does not persist changes. We'll also cover basic error handling patterns and a simple timeout strategy using Promise. race so your app can fail fast when a server is slow. By the end you will be able to wire a component to fetch data on mount, show loading and error states, and perform safe updates using the Fetch A P I. Think about one component you will add fetch to — what data will it request and how will you handle a 500 response? That question will guide your hands-on work.

These objectives describe the practical skills you will acquire using the Fetch A P I in React Native. First, you will be able to perform basic GET requests and display the returned JSON data using state and lifecycle hooks, which matters because most apps need remote data. Second, you will construct POST, PUT, and DELETE requests with a proper options object including method, headers, and body; this lets you create and update resources on an A P I and practice safe payload formatting. Third, you will parse responses correctly by awaiting response. json and using response. ok and response. status to detect HTTP errors — a common source of bugs if left unchecked. Fourth, you will implement basic error handling patterns and a simple timeout approach so your UI responds when networks fail or servers are slow. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic to help you remember the workflow and a milestone indicator showing when competency is verified. Together these skills let you build components that fetch, display, and update remote data reliably.

This second objectives panel breaks down practical checks and knowledge you will verify while coding. First, learn to set headers such as Content-Type and Authorization correctly so servers understand request formats and authenticate clients when needed. Second, practice updating local UI state after a successful response so the app feels responsive even when the remote server will not persist changes. Third, learn the distinction between network failures and HTTP errors: fetch rejects only on network failures but resolves for 404 or 500, so you must check response. ok and response. status. Fourth, understand the Fetch A P I's limits such as no builtin timeout and fewer global features compared to libraries; this will help you decide when to keep Fetch or switch to a library like Axios for advanced needs. These objectives keep your practice focused on verifiable behaviors and common pitfalls you'll encounter when building networked React Native components.

The Fetch A P I is a native JavaScript interface that defines how to perform HTTP network requests and work with the returned responses. In React Native it is available without additional libraries, and it gives you Request and Response objects that are more flexible than older techniques. A Request describes what you want to send — the URL, method, headers, and optional body — and the Response encapsulates status, headers, and body text. Practically, you call fetch with a URL and an optional options object. The fetch call returns a Promise that resolves to a Response. That Response is not yet the parsed JSON; you must call response. json and await it to obtain the object. A common misconception is to assume that fetch rejects on any HTTP error; in reality fetch rejects only on network failures, so you need to check response. ok to treat non-2xx responses as errors. For example, if you request a user list and the server responds 404, fetch resolves, and you must inspect response. status or response. ok and handle it. The takeaway is: fetch gives you control, but you must explicitly parse and verify responses before using the data. How will you check response. ok in your next component?

Let's walk through a practical GET example you can copy into a React Native component. The pattern uses useEffect to trigger the fetch once when the component mounts and useState to hold data, loading, and error states. Start by calling fetch with the endpoint URL. After awaiting the fetch, immediately check response. ok. If it's false, throw an error that your catch block can handle. Then await response. json to parse the body. Use the parsed array to set state and flip loading to false in finally. This approach keeps the UI responsive: you show an activity indicator while loading, display a readable error message if something goes wrong, and render the FlatList when data is present. A common pitfall is forgetting to await response. json, which leaves json as a Promise. Another subtle issue is not guarding the component for unmounted state in longer-lived requests, but for short example fetches this pattern is solid. Practice by fetching the sample users endpoint and rendering names and emails. After that, ask yourself: how do you surface a 500 error versus a network failure in your UI?

Parsing JSON from a Response is a two-step asynchronous process: first you await fetch which yields a Response object, then you call response. json which itself returns a Promise that resolves to the parsed JavaScript value. If you forget the second await, your variable will hold a Promise instead of the expected array or object; using that Promise like data will lead to runtime errors or empty renderings. In practice always write const json = await response. json(); and consider wrapping that in a try/catch if the server returns malformed JSON. Another detail: when an HTTP error occurs, the response body might contain an error payload; you can attempt to parse it with response. json but guard with try/catch because error bodies are not guaranteed to be JSON. A concrete strategy: after fetch resolves check response. ok, and if false attempt to parse errorBody = await response. json(). Use that information to build a user-facing message. The takeaway: treat parsing as part of the network flow and always await the parse step to avoid unresolved Promises in your state. Parsing JSON: await response.json() means response.json() returns a promise. always await it and guard against malformed or non-json error bodies.. In practical terms, why awaiting response.json matters and how to avoid the promise pitfall. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

To send or modify data you supply a second argument to fetch: the options object. This object commonly includes method, headers, and body. For JSON payloads set headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'} and use JSON. stringify to convert your JavaScript object into a string. For a POST you typically include the object you want to create, for PUT you send the updated resource, and for DELETE you can omit the body or include minimal identifying data. After calling fetch with these options, remember the same response checks and parsing patterns: if (! response. ok) handle the server-side error, otherwise await response. json for the response body. A frequent beginner mistake is to pass a plain object as body without stringifying, which leads to incorrect request payloads. Another gotcha is forgetting to include Authorization headers when endpoints require authentication. Practice by writing a createPost function that returns the created resource from the server and re-throws errors so the calling component can show a message or update local state. Which mutation will you implement first in your app and how will you verify it updated the UI?

A crucial part of robust networking is distinguishing between HTTP errors and network errors. Fetch only rejects the returned Promise on network-level failures, such as loss of connectivity or DNS issues. It resolves the Promise when a response is received from the server, even if that response is 404 or 500. That means you cannot rely on the catch block alone to detect bad status codes. Instead, after awaiting fetch, inspect response. ok, which is true for 2xx statuses and false otherwise. For HTTP errors you should parse the response body when helpful and throw a new Error to funnel handling through your catch block. For network errors fetch rejects, so the catch will run directly. A common beginner misconception is to expect fetch to throw on a 404; treating all non-ok responses the same way — by throwing after parsing any error body — yields consistent behavior. A practical pattern is to centralize this check in a small helper that throws when needed so your components only handle errors, not status logic. Handling HTTP errors vs Network errors means check response.ok and response.status after fetch; use try/catch to handle both parsed http errors and network failures consistently.. In practical terms, why fetch resolves for 4xx/5xx and how to treat each case. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fetch does not include a built-in timeout. If a server is slow or unresponsive, a fetch call can hang indefinitely. A simple and practical pattern to avoid this is to race the fetch call against a timeout Promise using Promise. race(). Create a Promise that rejects after a chosen duration and race it with the fetch Promise; when the timeout wins, you handle rejection and update UI accordingly. This approach gives you a fail-fast behavior and a place to show a retry UI. Be mindful that Promise. race does not cancel the original fetch; it only ignores the slower result. For real cancellation you may need AbortController in environments that support it, or a library that exposes cancellation. For basic apps, using Promise. race with a short timeout is usually sufficient to prevent hung network calls and create a predictable UX. Fetch is intentionally lightweight and built into JavaScript, making it perfect for simple GET and POST operations in many apps. However, it has limitations: no built-in timeout, no request cancellation in some environments without AbortController support, and no built-in retry or interceptor mechanisms for global behavior like attaching tokens or logging. Libraries such as Axios provide convenience features like automatic JSON transformation, request cancellation, timeout defaults, interceptors for authentication headers, and a consistent error shape. That said, adding a library increases bundle size and complexity. The rule of thumb is to start with Fetch for straightforward operations and add a library when you need advanced features such as global request/response interception, retries with backoff, or easier cancellation semantics. In many classroom projects Fetch is sufficient. Before adopting a library, list the problems you need solved — timeouts, retries, cancellation — and prefer the minimal tool that covers them. Here are practical patterns to adopt when you use Fetch across components. First, centralize repeated logic: create small helper functions that perform checked fetch, timeouts, or attach common headers so components stay focused on UI. Second, always show loading and error states and avoid assuming success. Third, use optimistic updates with rollback where appropriate for a snappy UX and use per-item spinners to avoid confusing the user. Fourth, parse error details when available so you can present meaningful messages instead of raw status codes. Finally, document and test your networking helpers for the edge cases seen in mobile environments: intermittent connectivity and slow responses. Let's summarize the core ideas to hold onto. First: Fetch returns a Response Promise; always await fetch, check response. ok or response. status, and then await response. json to parse the body. Second: For sending data use fetch(url, { method, headers, body: JSON. stringify(...) }) and ensure Content-Type is set to application/json so the server parses your payload correctly. Third: Fetch rejects only on network errors; for HTTP 4xx or 5xx you must inspect response. ok and throw an error to hit your catch block. These three pillars — correct request shape, explicit parsing, and manual HTTP error checks — make your networking code predictable and debuggable. Keep these in mind while implementing the hands-on To-Do example and when deciding whether to introduce helper wrappers or external libraries for more advanced needs.

A few additional best practices worth memorizing: centralize repeated fetch patterns into small helper functions so you avoid duplicating response checks and parsing logic. For user experience, always show loading indicators and clear error messages that are derived from parsed error bodies when available. Use Promise. race for a basic timeout and think about AbortController or a library when you need true cancellation. Finally, when choosing whether to pull in a library, ask whether you need global interceptors, retries, or consistent error shapes across many endpoints. If you do, a well-chosen HTTP library can save time; otherwise, the native Fetch A P I and a handful of helpers will remain lightweight and adequate for most classroom projects.
